title: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Where a single fossula occurs, we are usually told that it is a symptom of “bilaterality”; and this is in turn interpreted as an indication of a higher grade of organisation than is implied in the purely “radial symmetry” of the commoner types of coral. The mathematical aspect of the case gives no warrant for this interpretation.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VIII, “The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)”; topic “Septa and fossulae of corals”. Scope: rugose and other corals with septa meeting one another (Heterophyllia, Zaphrentis and allies)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch08-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The space-partition account of fossular geometry is testable from scans. The stronger conclusion that a fossula gives no evidence of bilaterality is an inference whose rival is underspecified and poorly served by fossil morphology alone.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct coral septal contact topology and test whether fossulae arise among predicted space-partition arrangements without covarying with independent measures of bilateral developmental organization.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Higher 'grade of organisation' has no clear modern metric.

Fossil specimens preserve geometry but little developmental evidence.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specimen images and scans can test whether fossulae look like ordinary completions of a trivalent septal network. The claim's denial that this indicates a higher bilateral grade is an inference about how the structure should be read, and packing compatibility does not uniquely decide it. Occurrence data help with sampling and do not supply the morphological test by themselves.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare fossula geometry in rugose corals with the septal graphs expected from three-way meetings, and test whether fossulae co-vary with other bilateral organ systems. Fossulae that match packing variants and occur without a broader bilateral suite would support the space-partition reading; fossulae aligned with a conserved bilateral plane and other bilateral traits would leave the higher-organization reading standing.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Showing that a fossula is a legal three-way packing does not rule out a biological bilateral function for the same chamber.

Septal junctions are often obscured in photographs of abraded fossils, and side-by-side organ-grade characters are not coded for these genera.
